{{Short description|Mechanical calculator capable of multiplying}}
[[Image:MillionaireCalculatorTopView.jpg|thumb|right|upright=2|<div align="center">''The Millionaire'' Calculator built by Egli around 1910</div>]]
'''The Millionaire''' was the first commercially successful [[mechanical calculator]] that could perform a direct multiplication. It was in production from 1893 to 1935 with a total of about five thousand machines manufactured.<ref>De Brabandere, L: ''Calculus'', page 166, Mardaga, 1995</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20060821084143/http://www-03.ibm.com/ibm/history/exhibits/attic3/attic3_035.html IBM historical archives]</ref>   

It was commercialized as "The Millionaire" in English speaking countries, '''"La Millionnaire"''' in French and '''"Millionär"''' in German speaking countries.

== History ==
The principle of a calculation machine with progressive transmission of tens was invented by [[Pafnuty Chebyshev|Chebyshev]] and demonstrated at the 1878 [[World's fair]]  in Paris. In 1881 Chebyshev demonstrated a model of the calculation machine with automatic multiplication but did not take out a patent for it.

In 1834 [[Luigi Torchi (inventor)|Luigi Torchi]] of Milan invented a direct multiplication machine.<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://history-computer.com/MechanicalCalculators/19thCentury/Torchi.html|title = Luigi Torchi|date = 4 January 2021|access-date = 25 November 2016|archive-date = 9 December 2020|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201209034406/https://history-computer.com/MechanicalCalculators/19thCentury/Torchi.html|url-status = dead}}</ref> The first patented multiplying machines was due to [[Edmund Barbour]]<ref>[http://history-computer.com/MechanicalCalculators/19thCentury/Barbour.html Barbour machine] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201119150548/http://history-computer.com/MechanicalCalculators/19thCentury/Barbour.html |date=2020-11-19 }} on History of Computer website</ref> (1872), [[Ramón Verea]]<ref>[http://history-computer.com/MechanicalCalculators/19thCentury/Verea.html Verea machine] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200704034555/http://history-computer.com/MechanicalCalculators/19thCentury/Verea.html |date=2020-07-04 }} on History of Computer website</ref> (1878) and [[Léon Bollée]] (1889).<ref>[http://history-computer.com/MechanicalCalculators/19thCentury/Bollee.html Bollée machine] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201105073830/http://history-computer.com/MechanicalCalculators/19thCentury/Bollee.html |date=2020-11-05 }} on History of Computer website</ref> The Bollée machine could be considered the direct ancestor of the ''Millionaire''.

Designed by [[Otto Steiger (engineer)|Otto Steiger]], a Swiss engineer, the moving carriage of the Millionaire has a 20 decimal digit accumulator that shows the product after multiplication and into which dividend is entered prior to division.  The 10-digit multiplicand or divisor is entered on the sliders
(or keyboard, on later models) above the carriage, while successive digits of the multiplier or quotient are entered with a push-button lever on the upper left.  A large control knob on the upper right can be set to add, multiply, divide or subtract positions.<ref>Henry J. Kennedy, [https://books.google.com/books?id=zk88AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA555 An Ingenious Calculating Machine], ''American Machinist,'' Nov. 1, 1906; pages 555–563.</ref>

The ''Millionaire'' was first patented in Germany in 1892. Patents were issued in [[France]], [[Switzerland]], [[Canada]] and the [[United States]] in 1893, and production started in 1893.<ref>Steiger, Otto Steiger, Multiplying or Dividing Machine, {{US patent|538710}}, issued May 7, 1895.</ref> From 1899 to 1935 [[Hans W. Egli]] of [[Zürich]] handled the machine.  The American agent for the Millionaire was W. A. Morschhauser of New York.  A detailed investigation by Gerald Saudan established that 5,099 "Millionaire" had been manufactured overall in four decades, rather than the commonly quoted 4,655 units.<ref>G. Saudan, ''Swiss Calculating Machines. H.-W. Egli A.-G. A success story'', Gerald Saudan Publishing, Yens (Switzerland), 2017, ISBN 978-2-8399-2175-6.</ref><ref>The "4,655" figure comes from [https://web.archive.org/web/20060821084143/http://www-03.ibm.com/ibm/history/exhibits/attic3/attic3_035.html IBM Computer Museum], but Millionaire [http://www.rechnerlexikon.de/it/upload/f/fb/Millionaire-SN6455.jpg SN 6455] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230213082836/http://www.rechnerlexikon.de/it/upload/f/fb/Millionaire-SN6455.jpg |date=2023-02-13 }} and [[:File:Millionaire6482.jpg|SN 6482]] exist.</ref><ref>New Machinery and Processes: [https://books.google.com/books?id=RZZAAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA177 The "Millionaire" Calculator], ''Textile World Record'', Vol. 34, No. 1 (Oct. 1907); page 177.</ref>

The Millionaire was advertised as being the "only calculating machine on the market ... that requires but one turn of the crank ... for each figure in the multiplier or quotient," making it the fastest calculator available.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=7P8-AQAAMAAJ&pg=RA1-PA18 The Millionaire Calculating Machine], advertisement, ''The Executive Economist'', Vol. 1, No. 4 (April 1911); back cover.</ref>  Advertising from 1913 claims that the United States government had purchased over 100 Millionaire calculators.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=utkxAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA293 "Endorsed by the U.S.Government"], advertisement, ''Business'', Vol. XXXI, No. 5 (Nov. 1913); page 293.</ref>

== Competition ==
All mechanical calculators commercialized prior to the Millionaire, like the [[arithmometer]], the [[Odhner Arithmometer|Odhner arithmometer]] or the [[comptometer]] were simple adding machines; they implemented multiplication by continued addition under operator control. In 1889, [[Léon Bollée]], in France, invented a machine that required only one turn of the crank handle to multiply the number entered on the sliders by a multiplier number. This was accomplished by creating a ''mechanical representation'' of the multiplication table which could be read and used by the machine. The manufacturing cost of Bollée's machine was too high and the production was discontinued after a few units. The Millionaire was built with the same target of direct mechanical multiplication in mind.<ref>Martin, E: ''[[The Calculating Machines]]'', page 119, Charles Babbage Institute, 1992</ref>

In first decades of 20th century two other machines with direct multiplication were produced: the Moon-Hopkins<ref>[http://www.rechnerlexikon.de/it/artikel/Burroughs-Moon-Hopkins Burroughs-Moon-Hopkins] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230213152016/http://www.rechnerlexikon.de/it/artikel/Burroughs-Moon-Hopkins |date=2023-02-13 }} on Rechnerlexikon</ref> and Kuhrt-US.<ref>[http://www.rechenmaschinen-illustrated.com/pictures_1921.htm#Kuhrt%20US Kuhrt-US] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230901154903/http://www.rechenmaschinen-illustrated.com/pictures_1921.htm#Kuhrt%20US |date=2023-09-01 }} on Rechenmaschinen lllustrated</ref> These two companies were then taken over by [[Burroughs Corporation|Burroughs]]<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.burroughsinfo.com/historical-timeline.html |title=Historical Timeline - Burroughs Adding Machine Company |access-date=2024-12-28 |archive-date=2022-03-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220324193734/http://www.burroughsinfo.com/historical-timeline.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and Brunsviga.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.arithmeum.uni-bonn.de/sammlungen/rechnen-einst/objekt.html?tx_arithinventory&#91;object&#93;=11366 |title=Kuhrt AB |access-date=2024-12-28 |archive-date=2024-06-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240625124032/https://www.arithmeum.uni-bonn.de/sammlungen/rechnen-einst/objekt.html?tx_arithinventory%5Bobject%5D=11366 |url-status=live }}</ref> These machines filled quite a different niche from the Millionaire. They were book-keeping machines with printing features, and were too unwieldy to perform divisions and complex computations. The Millionaire was better suited for technical computations.

This machine weighed some 20 kilograms and was the size of a small suitcase, occupying half of a desk. It was as easy to operate as the Arithmometer, which had established a standard since the mid-XIXth century.
